title: Minister Anand meets with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V - canada.ca
content: The Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, met with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V in Vancouver today to discuss shared priorities related to international development, economic partnerships, affordable housing and regional security. July 25, 2026 - Vancouver, British Columbia - Global Affairs Canada The Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, met with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V in Vancouver today to discuss shared priorities related to international development, economic partnerships, affordable housing and regional security. Minister Anand welcomed the progress of the implementation of the Joint declaration between Prime Minister Mark Carney and His Highness the Aga Khan of March 2026 and noted the importance of maintaining momentum on its implementation. The Minister also highlighted the success of the Generations multi-generational housing initiative across Canada, led by the Ismaili Council for Canada, and underscored that affordable housing remains a priority for the Government of Canada. Minister Anand and the Aga Khan discussed the housing partnership announced under the Joint Declaration, a clear example of practical cooperation between Canada and the Ismaili Imamat and welcomed the Memorandum of Understanding between Build Canada Homes and the Ismaili Council for Canada, dedicated to  focused on advancing affordable multi-generational housing and community infrastructure projects across Canada. The Minister also highlighted the continued cooperation through the FinDev Canada-Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development Memorandum of Understanding, which outlines a shared commitment to cooperate and explore potential investment opportunities in infrastructure, renewable energy, agriculture and financial services. The Minister also recognized the Aga Khan Development Network's (AKDN) long-standing presence and expertise in regions facing complex challenges, including Syria, and highlighted its important development partnerships in Pakistan and East Africa, expressing appreciation for its work improving the quality of life through initiatives that address social and economic challenges facing local communities. Minister Anand concluded by recognizing the long-standing contributions of the Ismaili community in Canada through volunteerism, civic engagement, philanthropy and investment in communities across the country, and reaffirmed Canada's commitment to deepening its partnership with the Ismaili Imamat and the AKDN, including through continued collaboration to advance stability, resilience and sustainable development. The voter‑approved half‑cent sales tax generated $26.7 million in revenue during Fiscal Year 2024‑25 and invested nearly $15 million in transportation improvements countywide. The audited financial statements included in the report show, “total revenue: $26,762,905… total expenditure: $14,984,261.” Since Measure V took effect in 2017, the program has produced more than $200 million for road repairs, mobility upgrades and public transit. This year’s report highlights dozens of projects completed between July 2024 and June 2025, ranging from street rehabilitation and bridge replacements to sidewalk infill, bicycle infrastructure and intersection improvements. Every incorporated city in Merced County received Measure V funding, along with county‑maintained roads and regional corridors. Countywide, Measure V supported a wide range of transportation improvements. Examples highlighted in the report include the Lorraine Street Bridge replacement in Dos Palos, Palm Avenue rehabilitation in Merced County, and multiple sidewalk and street repairs in Merced, Livingston and Los Banos. The report also shows $2.3 million spent on alternative transportation modes, including bicycle and pedestrian improvements and investments in zero‑emission transit vehicles. Public transportation continues to play a major role in countywide mobility. Measure V’s free‑fare program provided 202,019 rides on The Bus’ fixed‑route system last fiscal year. Of those trips, 133,358 were taken by seniors, 63,366 by ADA‑eligible passengers and 5,295 by veterans. The report states that the program “helped residents access employment, medical care, shopping and other essential services.” MCAG Executive Director Stacie Guzman said the annual report demonstrates the value of the voter‑approved measure. “Every Measure V dollar spent represents an investment that Merced County residents made in their own communities,” Guzman said. The full 2026 On the MoVe report is available at mcagov.org/onthemove, with free printed copies in English and Spanish at all Merced County city halls and the county administration building.

title: Allison to supply transmissions for about 3,000 German EAGLE V armored vehicles, with option for 2,000 more - Defence Industry Europe
content: Allison Transmission will supply fully automatic transmissions for about 3,000 General Dynamics European Land Systems EAGLE V armored vehicles ordered by Germany’s armed forces. The Bundeswehr contract with GDELS also includes an option for up to 2,000 additional vehicles. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2027 and will cover EAGLE V 4×4 command-and-control vehicles and EAGLE V 6×6 medium armored ambulances. Allison’s 2500 Specialty Series fully automatic transmission will remain the exclusive transmission option across all EAGLE variants. The units will be delivered through Sterki AG, Allison’s authorized dealer and distributor in Switzerland. The order extends a supply relationship between Allison and GDELS that has supported the EAGLE vehicle family for more than two decades. Since production of the EAGLE IV began in 2005, every EAGLE model has used Allison 2500 SP transmissions as standard equipment. Germany has procured about 670 EAGLE IV and EAGLE V vehicles since 2008. The Bundeswehr has also ordered 80 EAGLE V 6×6 protected ambulance vehicles, with deliveries beginning in May 2025. The latest procurement will significantly increase the number of EAGLE vehicles entering German military service. “Allison is honored that GDELS entrusts the reliability and performance of our transmissions,” said Taner Gider, Executive Director, EMEA Sales at Allison Transmission. “This performance is backed by Allison’s global support network that delivers the specialized expertise and response capabilities necessary to maintain operational readiness when every second counts.” “Allison’s decades of experience in defense applications, backed by world class manufacturing and engineering excellence, has made it the preferred choice in the industry,” Gider said. Allison said its SP Series is engineered for demanding applications and is designed to provide power transfer and vehicle control in difficult terrain. The EAGLE V 4×4 serves as a mobile command center and supports tactical coordination through communication and command systems. The EAGLE V 6×6 ambulance transports rescue teams and can operate as a mobile medical unit when staffed with emergency physicians. The Allison 2500 SP transmission is used across defense, national security and emergency-service applications. The new order expands Allison’s role in the EAGLE program as GDELS prepares to deliver a much larger protected-vehicle fleet to Germany from 2027. title: All-Ireland football final: Kerry v Mayo - triumph, pain and 'the curse' - BBC
content: Kerry were victors when they last met Mayo in an All-Ireland final back in 2006 In the build-up to last year's All-Ireland final, former Kerry captain Dara Ó Cinnéide pointed out "nobody has lost more finals than Kerry". It's true, as while the Kingdom lead the way on the roll of honour with 39 Sam Maguire triumphs, their 24 defeats on Gaelic football's biggest day is greater than any other county. Cork are next in that unwanted bracket with 16, but just one behind - level with Galway - sits Mayo. The Yew County must go back 75 years for the last of their three All-Ireland titles, defending the crown they had won the previous season, but while All-Ireland success has eluded them since, a return to the final was 44 years in the making. In 1989, led by the late John O'Mahony, Mayo rolled into Croke Park to face a Cork side that had fallen short in the previous two finals against Meath - the second of those after a replay. Perhaps there was a sense that it was the Rebels' time, but Mayo had their chances, only to fall to a three-point defeat. It would prove to be the first of 11 disappointments on final day. Watch live on BBC Two, BBC Sport website & app from 15:00 They were back seven years later, thanks to a semi-final win over Kerry who were ready to challenge again after a number of years in the wilderness, but after Colm Coyle's late punt hopped off the ground and over the bar to force a draw, Meath won a replay that was marred by an early brawl. Certainly, there was an element of fortune in Meath's equaliser in the drawn game, but could it be something a lot deeper for Mayo? A curse, perhaps? As the story - or myth - goes, following their 1951 win and on their way home on to Castlebar on an open-back lorry, the team's boisterous celebrations interrupted a funeral taking place in Foxford, just outside Ballina with the presiding priest laying a curse that Mayo would not win an All-Ireland title any member of the team was alive. Whether that is fact or folklore remains unclear, but Mayo's fortunes on All-Ireland final day have not improved since. The following year, they returned to the decider against Kerry who would make up for the previous year's semi-final reverse with a three-point win. It would not be misfortune for Mayo, but the brilliance of Maurice Fitzgerald that was the difference, with the Cahersiveen man kicking nine points on the day. Those two meetings between the counties would prove to be the beginning of a new-found rivalry. Kerry won the first of two All-Ireland finals in three years against Mayo in 2004 Kerry would return to the top in 2000, marking the start of a successful decade as Sam Maguire would return to the Kingdom on five occasions, with three further final defeats in this time. In 2004, Mayo were back in the final to meet them and while Alan Dillon netted an early goal, the game would quickly get away from them as Colm Cooper goaled at the other end on a day in which he and Ó Cinnéide starred in an emphatic win as Jack O'Connor led Kerry to his first title as manager. Two years later, Mayo stunned Dublin the last four with Ciaran McDonald landing a sublime winner, but it was the same old story in the final as an early goal blitz paved the way for another handsome win for Kerry. While O'Connor stood down at the end of 2006, Pat O'Shea would guide them to another title title the following season - the last time Kerry achieved back to back All-Irelands, only for Tyrone to deny them three-in-a-row the following year - a repeat of the 2005 decider. Mayo were winners in the 2017 semi-final after a replay As that great Kerry team's powers began to fade by the end of the decade, Mayo would find a new nemesis as after defeat by Donegal in 2012, Dublin would account for them in the 2013 decider, again in 2016 after a replay that was largely down to two first-half own goals in the drawn game, while Dean Rock would break their hearts with a winning free at the death in the 2017 final. However, Kerry and Mayo would serve up some incredible semi-final drama in the 2010s as after Kieran O'Leary salvaged a draw for Kerry at Croke Park, the Kingdom would win after extra-time in a thriller at Limerick's Gaelic Grounds. Three years later at the same stage, it was roles reversed as Paddy Durcan rescued a draw for Mayo who finished the job in the replay thanks to goals from current manager Andy Moran and Diarmuid O'Connor. While the counties lost two All-Ireland finals apiece since that game, Kerry have added two more titles in the third coming of O'Connor. They sides swapped wins in 2022 and 2023, Kerry now an established force led by the talents of the Cliffords, the Geaneys, Gavin White and Sean O'Shea. Mayo contain many survivors of their most recent final defeat by Tyrone in 2021, but a fresh crop have also emerged in Kobe McDonald, Darragh Beirne, Eoin McGreal and Cian McHale. Will the ghosts of All-Ireland finals past continue to haunt Mayo and Kerry cement their place at the top, or will the 75 years of hurt finally come to an end against a county that has handed them three of those 11 defeats since 1951? Sunday will be a day to remember for one set of supporters, while the other will revisit that sense of devastation both know only too well on All-Ireland final day. As for the 'curse'? Well, the last member of the Mayo 1951 panel, Dr Mick Loftus, passed away in 2023. title: Socialists v. the Senate - The Mining Journal -
content: Political parties tend to harshly reject the idea that they are a threat to the constitutional order, but the Democratic Socialists of America are making it part of their brand. The DSA has released a new program that, besides contemplating the advent of a classless society, calls for abolishing the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court. This is literally a revolutionary program to topple the American system as we have known it since 1789. It’s the kind of thing you might expect after angry rebels mount the barricades in Washington, D.C., and overthrow the government. It makes proposals to abolish the filibuster seem trifling in comparison and even makes court-packing look relatively moderate. The proposal to kill off the world’s greatest deliberative body has gotten the most attention. New York City’s DSA co-chair, Gustavo Gordillo, went on Fox News to explain that the senate is “undemocratic,” while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said that she opposes the filibuster and elements of the Senate that “were founded on Jim Crow.” Contrary to Gordillo, the Senate is a democratic institution; no one wins a Senate seat without getting more votes than his or her opponent. Yet, part of its role in our system is to serve as a check on popular passions. At the institution’s inception, state legislatures appointed senators. Those days are long gone -- the 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, requires direct election -- but six-year terms and staggered elections give the Senate more insulation from the transient currents of public sentiment than the House of Representatives. Then there are the senate rules that put an emphasis on consensus and delay. AOC sounded confused when she cited Senate practices created under Jim Crow, the system of formalized racial discrimination that arose about 100 years after the creation of the Senate. It’s true that the filibuster was used as a tool to attempt to block landmark civil rights legislation, without ultimate success. But the filibuster is an instrument of every minority party in the Senate trying to block the agenda of a president of the opposing party, very much including Senate Democrats arrayed against President Trump today. The Senate has another function, which is giving small states equal representation with large states. This is the source of the charge that it is undemocratic. Why should Wyoming, population roughly 600,000, have as many senators as California, population nearly 40 million? This is meant, though, to keep large states from having overwhelming influence on the nation’s governance, and to give easy-to-ignore places a say in the nation’s affairs. For proportional representation, there’s the House; California has 52 members of Congress, whereas Wyoming has one. All this said, regardless of the merits, the Constitution deems the provision of equal senators for the states un-amendable: “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” This suggests that the dissolution of the constitutional system couldn’t be achieved by constitutional means, since the Founders didn’t supply a readily available self-destruct button for their brilliant handiwork. Not that the DSA cares. What they are seeking would, in some ways, be a return to the Articles of Confederation, under which we had a unicameral legislature and neither a presidency nor federal courts. But this made for a very weak central government, while the DSA wants an overweening Washington, D.C., shorn of the inherent checks on the popular will that come with a multi-layered federal system. In short, it hopes for what Lord Hailsham, in his criticism of the British parliamentary system, famously called an “elective dictatorship.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a speech last week in which he inveighed against left-wing extremists who seek to destroy rather than build, targeting “the physical embodied symbols of power and invention and achievement.” He might have added to the target list, with a nod to the DSA, the U.S. constitutional order; the socialists have met the enemy — and it is our own longstanding, highly successful governing institutions. 249 W. title: Section V flag football stars rack up all-state honors - Democrat and Chronicle
content: As high school flag football continues to grow in popularity, so does the number of Section V players earning recognition among the state's best. The New York State Sportswriters Association put together the first set of all-state flag football teams in 2025. This year's selections include seven players at Section V schools named first team all-state, one more than last season. Webster Schroeder quarterback Emma Rascoe has completed her high school playing days as a two-time member of the Class B all-state first team offense. Rascoe, the 2026 Democrat and Chronicle All-Greater Rochester Player of the Year, finished with 63 touchdown passes and 78 total touchdowns during her senior season as Webster Schroeder went 14-2. She finished with 4,729 all-purpose yards, including 3,776 passing yards, while helping the Warriors win the Section V Class B championship. The Warriors were state champions in 2025. Bishop Kearney standout Nela Lopusanova, a three-time AGR first team member, and East Rochester defensive star Payton Kinney earned Class C first-team all-state honors for the second consecutive year. title: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware - PetaPixel
content: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware Canon released new firmware updates for the EOS R6 Mark III and EOS R6 V cameras this week. Arguably the biggest addition of all is the ability to shoot with flash on the R6 V. While the Canon EOS R6 V is undoubtedly better suited to video than photography, the camera does have many of the same still photography capabilities as the R6 III, albeit without that camera’s mechanical shutter. It was this lack of a shutter that presumably led to the R6 V shipping a couple of months ago without the ability to use flash. The R6 III, for example, is not compatible with flash when set to its electronic shutter option. For that matter, the R6 V is still very limited with flash. Although Canon doesn’t offer specifics on its R6 V firmware page, DPReview notes that flash on the R6 V is limited to a maximum sync speed of just 1/60s, which is very slow. It is also worth recalling that the R6 V lacks a traditional five-pin hotshoe. It works with Canon’s Multi-Interface-equipped Speedlite units, but not traditional flashes. Nonetheless, it’s nice to have the option to use flash on the R6 V, as that was a rather notable omission for hybrid shooters. Other improvements introduced in firmware 1.1.0 include support for Canon’s new BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller, support for Canon’s SDK, bug fixes, and improved “operational stability,” the most popular update in firmware history. The Canon EOS R6 III is also now at version 1.1.0. Compatibility with the BR-E2 has been added, and Canon has introduced SDK support for the R6 III, too. Canon has also added the option to set autofocus for close-up demos to the camera’s menus and the option to set a grid display during movie recording, features that were already available in the R6 V. Canon also addressed some potentially frustrating bugs, like FTP errors, an issue with interval shooting, and a USB problem. And, as always, operational stability is better now. Firmware 1.1.0 for the Canon EOS R6 V and the EOS R6 III is available to download now. title: 2026 Aston Martin Vanquish 25 First Look: A Silver Anniversary of V-12 Power - MotorTrend
content:
Available as a coupe or Volante convertible, the Vanquish 25 celebrates 25 years of Aston Martin’s flagship. Twenty-five years is a long time for a nameplate to stick around, especially one created in the early 21st century. But the Aston Martin Vanquish has indeed reached that silver anniversary, a milestone being marked with a special model available as either a coupe or convertible. Production will be limited to just 50 examples—25 of each body style—and feature bespoke details and paintwork created by Q, Aston Martin’s in-house customization house. The brilliant silver coating the cars is called Q Skye Silver, an exclusive paint developed just for the Vanquish 25. It shines brightly under the sun but takes on a much darker tone in the shadows. This contrast helps accentuate the car’s sculptural body lines. The Vanquish 25 also gets special side sills and metal-foil accents that include on the Aston Martin wordmark on the rear of the car. Stainless steel side strakes, unique exhaust tips, Vanquish 25 badging, and exclusive 21-inch wheels complete the exterior. Inside, the cabin of the Vanquish 25 features unique perforation patterns and split finishes. The headrests have embroidered Vanquish 25 logos and the Aston Martin wordmark is laser-etched into the trim. The bright red start/stop button is surrounded by unique trim, and black Alcantara lines the roof above occupants in both 2+2 and true two-seater configurations. Of course, the star of the show, and what makes the Vanquish special, is its Aston Martin V-12 engine. Under the hood of the 2026 Vanquish 25 sits the latest version of the 5.2-liter twin-turbo V-12, the AE31. Although this engine first debuted in the DB11 in 2016, enhancements made in 2024 for the current Vanquish’s debut strengthened the block, improved turbocharger response, and raised output to 824 horsepower and 738 lb-ft of torque. With that much power on tap, the Vanquish coupe is capable of a 0–60 mph time of 3.3 seconds and an 11.2-second quarter-mile at 132.5 mph in MotorTrend testing, as well as a top speed of 214 mph. The 2026 Aston Martin Vanquish 25 is set to make its physical debut during Monterey Car Week next month. Deliveries are scheduled to begin toward the end of this year. title: C.H. Robinson to appeal $604M verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior - Transport Topics
content: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] Freight brokerage giant C.H. Robinson is appealing a $604 million jury verdict handed down July 24 in a case that found it liable for a 2021 fatal crash in Mississippi. The outcome of Lipe v. Lupus Superior comes less than three months after a landmark Supreme Court ruling affirmed that negligent hiring claims against freight brokers can proceed under state law. PREMIUM: Small brokers and carriers face pressure after SCOTUS ruling The case, tried in Dallas County Court in Texas, centered on whether C.H. Robinson and motor carrier Lupus Superior were liable for negligence relating to a crash that killed three people and injured two others. “We extend our deepest sympathies to everyone affected by this tragic accident,” Dorothy Capers, chief legal officer at C.H. Robinson, told Transport Topics. “Every loss of life on our nation’s highways is one too many. We strongly disagree with the verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior, LLC, et al. and will immediately appeal.” C.H. Robinson asserts that it should not be held liable and did not act negligently. The company pointed out that the carrier had safely delivered nearly 270 loads for its customers and held a satisfactory rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration when it was selected. “Safety is core to how we operate and always has been,” Capers said. “We go beyond federal requirements and apply multiple layers of safety and risk criteria that we continuously re-evaluate and strengthen. The shipments we arrange overwhelmingly move without incident, with one serious accident claim filed for every 500 million miles driven on our customers’ loads.” Capers views the decision as reinforcing ongoing calls for the federal government to better address road safety. She also noted that the carrier maintained a satisfactory rating even after a federal review of the accident. C.H. Robinson, she pointed out, does not employ drivers. “The extreme nature of this verdict means it is even more imperative that Congress and the federal government act with urgency to establish clear and proper accountabilities across the transportation industry that enhance highway safety and support the uninterrupted flow of goods across the United States,” Capers said. Jennifer Lipe, Benjamin Brewer and Rhoderick Coleman burned to death in their vehicles after a Lupus Superior truck crashed into stopped traffic in Mississippi. Rodney Hawkins and Gabrielle Broussard were injured. The plaintiffs in the case were represented by law firm Arnold & Itkin. The largest 3PLs in North America continued to face volatile business conditions last year, from compressed margins to tariff-driven supply chain upheaval. Read more “No amount of money will replace the parents and spouses who burned to death in this horrible crash,” said Roland Christensen, attorney at Arnold & Itkin. “But this verdict is a message to C.H. Robinson and the brokering industry that their dangerous practices are not acceptable.” Christensen claimed the company refused to accept responsibility for hiring a motor carrier with a history of safety alerts. C.H. Robinson also was at the center of the Supreme Court’s Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II ruling, issued May 14. RELATED: C.H. Robinson sees clarity in Montgomery decision That case challenged whether federal law that restricts states from regulating brokerage services protects freight brokers from state lawsuits over negligent hirings. The high court’s decision is notable for undoing what had been a presumed protection for brokers. C.H. Robinson expressed optimism at the time that the ruling would lead to needed legal clarity. C.H. Robinson ranks No. 2 on the Transport Topics Top 100 list of the largest logistics companies in North America.

title: Why Mobley v. Workday has far-reaching legal impacts for HR leaders - HR Executive
content: As previously covered, the litigation and regulatory risks facing HR departments adopting artificial intelligence are continuing to emerge. The initial wave of AI-related risks facing HR departments tested legal theories focused on discrimination, and the second wave has focused on the use of AI to create “consumer reports” about job applicants in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). Now, courts have started reaching the merits of the first wave of AI-related discrimination cases, which will likely open the door for similar suits in the future. This article discusses the recent court decision addressing AI-related discrimination claims and what employers can do to mitigate these risks. In February 2023, a class action was filed against Workday (Mobley v. Workday, Inc.), alleging that Workday’s AI-driven HR tools, such as HiredScore AI and Candidate Skills Match, discriminate on the basis of race, age and disability in violation of several federal and California laws. The case alleges that Workday’s AI recommendation system, Candidate Skills Match, which scored and ranked individuals, produced discriminatory outcomes at scale across hundreds of employer-customers. The court previously conditionally certified an Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) class of persons aged 40 and older whose applications were processed by Workday’s AI recommendation system from September 2020 to the present. Earlier this year, the court also allowed a claim against Workday’s AI recommendation system to proceed under California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). In addition to letting the FEHA claim proceed, the court also held that the FEHA claim can extend to Workday’s AI-powered hiring tools used by non-California employers to evaluate non-California applicants. The court’s most significant holding is that FEHA reaches Workday’s conduct as a California-based agent engaging in allegedly discriminatory screening on behalf of employer-customers nationwide. title: OBITUARY: Carol V. Cote - Marblehead Current
content: It is with great sadness that we announce the peaceful passing of Carol V. Cote on July 6, surrounded by the love of her family. Carol grew up in Manasquan, New Jersey, where she developed the warmth, kindness and sense of humor that defined her throughout her life. She attended Centenary College in New Jersey, where she formed lifelong friendships and embraced the values that guided her through the years. Throughout her career, Carol worked as an administrative assistant at several leading financial institutions, where she was known for her professionalism, dedication, kindness and unwavering work ethic. She also devoted part of her career to special education, where her patience, compassion and gentle spirit made a meaningful difference in the lives of the students she served. Carol spent many happy years living in Narragansett, Rhode Island, where she treasured summers at the beach and created countless cherished memories with family and friends. She later returned to Marblehead, a community she loved and was proud to call home. Carol possessed a creative and entrepreneurial spirit. In the 1980s, she and a close friend started a small business designing and selling hand-stenciled belts. She took great pride in their work and found joy in sharing her artistic talents with others. An avid gardener, Carol found great happiness in cultivating beautiful gardens and was a proud member of the Marblehead Garden Club. She was also an accomplished golfer who loved the game and treasured the many friendships it brought throughout her life. Whether tending her garden, spending time on the golf course, or enjoying a day at the beach, Carol embraced every moment with enthusiasm, gratitude and joy. Carol was predeceased by parents George and Elizabeth Vogel of Sarasota; her beloved husband, Ralph Cote; her stepson, Christopher Cote; and her sister and brother-in-law, Whitney and Ray Armstrong of Manasquan, New Jersey. Above all, Carol cherished her family. She is survived by her sister, Elizabeth “Bitsy” Graham, and her husband, Tim Graham, of Ashland, Massachusetts; her daughter, Erin Mahan, and her longtime partner, Andrew Brittain; her son, Greg Mahan; her grandchildren, Matthew Mahan and Nora Mahan; her stepchildren and their spouses, Donna and John Gaumond, Michelle and Ken Adams, David and Betsy Cote, Doug and Jennifer Cote, Lisa Cote, Paul and Paula Richard, Susan Cote Bleuel, and Laurie Cote; her 23 step-grandchildren; her 21 step-great-grandchildren; and many extended family members and dear friends, all of whom were touched by her love, generosity and wonderful sense of humor. Those who wish to honor Carol’s memory may make a donation to the Alzheimer’s Association to support research, care and hope for families affected by Alzheimer’s disease. Honda Motor on Thursday confirmed a next-generation model of its Ridgeline pickup truck will be produced in the U.S. following a temporary production stoppage later this year. The future of the midsize pickup truck has been in flux amid reports that there could be a production pause coming due to the vehicle not meeting California emissions regulations. The Japanese automaker on Thursday said there will be a temporary production stoppage for the pickup truck later this year at the Alabama plant that produces the vehicle, with assembly returning to the facility within two years, likely in 2028. “The goal is to continue to serve those customers who’ve been loyal to the Ridgeline,” Lance Woelfer, vice president of auto sales at American Honda Motor, told CNBC. “But one of the things that we want to bring forward in the future is increased ruggedness of that vehicle, even more capability.” Woelfer declined to comment on whether the more rugged capability will include the vehicle moving from a car-based production process to a more traditional truck assembly, known as “body-on-frame,” which is how most trucks are built in the U.S. “That’s been an important part of its history. Whether or not it’s part of its future, I won’t get into that,” Woelfer said. “This is a step forward for the Ridgeline that I think everybody will appreciate.” Expanding the capability of the Ridgeline, which is more known for smooth driving than ruggedness, could assist in expanding the vehicle’s buyers. Sales of the Ridgeline were down about 3% during the first half of the year. The company has sold between roughly 41,000 and 52,000 Ridgelines annually since 2021. That compares with more than 270,000 units sold of the segment-leading Toyota Tacoma in 2025. Honda’s confirmation of the new pickup comes as its CR-V compact crossover led U.S. auto sales through the first half of the year for the first time ever. CR-V sales increased roughly 6% compared with last year as the Ford F-Series pickups and Toyota Rav4 crossover, which have led sales in recent years, dealt with production bottlenecks. Rockabilly talisman Brian Setzer is rarely seen without a big-bodied Gretsch guitar, but there’s an unlikely Gibson in his collection that's giving his favorite hollowbody a run for its money. Setzer has been on a difficult road to recovery following struggles with an autoimmune disease that left him unable to play guitar. Now he’s just days away from returning to the stage with the Stray Cats on a US tour, where his Gretsch guitars will once again shine. But when asked in the new issue of Guitar World about what he’d play if he were banned from using his beloved Gretsch 6120s, he revealed there was only one choice. “I recently bought a ’59 Flying V and a ’59 Les Paul,” he says. “I bought them because, fortunately, I had the money saved up, and I wanted to see what the fuss was all about. “Now, the Les Paul is a beautifully built guitar, and it plays beautifully. I cannot fault it. The only thing is, it’s not my tone. It’s not my particular sound. I couldn’t bring it on stage or even record with it. It’s just not me, even though it’s a joy to play.” The Flying V, though, is another matter. It’s got Setzer drooling. “It sounds like the Gretsch,” he purrs. “I kid you not, man! I played a Gretsch and then played the ’59 Flying V, and I couldn’t tell the difference. The only other guitar that could take the place of the Gretsch would be an older Flying V. It sounded so similar – I couldn’t believe it.” All the latest guitar news, interviews, lessons, reviews, deals and more, direct to your inbox! On the surface, a Gibson Flying V is far removed from a 6120 – one’s hollow-bodied, and one’s solid–bodied, for a start – and the instrument’s biggest players, from Michael Schenker to Leslie West and James Hetfield, aren’t exactly of Setzer’s ilk. Yet… “It had the balls, it had that twang,” Setzer confirms. “The Les Paul doesn’t have it, but the old Flying V does. It’s the weirdest thing.” But don’t expect to see it on the road with the Stray Cats any time soon: “I’m afraid to take it out,” he admits. “It’s worth so much money.” Elsewhere in his GW interview, Setzer recalled the lesson he learned from playing Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Strat after a tough tour together. title: Public opinion on abortion has shifted 4 years after Dobbs decision overturned Roe v. Wade - The Conversation
content: It’s been four years since the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization overturned Roe v. Wade, ending the federal constitutional right to abortion. In the immediate aftermath of the decision, national attention centered on implementation of state bans and a rapidly shifting legal landscape. But four years later, one of the most impactful developments has been less visible: a significant, sustained and politically consequential shift in public opinion. In the wake of Dobbs, the debate over abortion rights did not simply return to the states. It fundamentally altered how many Americans think about the issue and how they vote. In our recently published book, “Not Going Back: Public Opinion on Abortion in Post-Dobbs America,” we examined how and why these changes have occurred, and what they mean for U.S. politics. We believe the shift could have real consequences for the November 2026 midterms. Drawing on several nationally representative surveys conducted before and after Dobbs, we examined how Americans’ abortion attitudes, political priorities and voting behavior have changed in response to the most significant shift in abortion policy in half a century. For nearly 50 years after Roe, public opinion on abortion was remarkably stable. In 1975, Gallup found support for legal abortion in certain circumstances at 54% and support for a ban in all circumstances at 22%. In 2021 – the year before the Dobbs decision – these figures were virtually the same: 48% and 19%, respectively. Despite heated political rhetoric, most Americans held nuanced views. They were neither fully anti-abortion nor fully pro-abortion. Instead, they supported legal abortion in some circumstances and not in others. That underlying stability shaped both policy and politics for decades. Republicans were able to rally a committed core of supporters around opposition to Roe, while the underlying constitutional right to access abortion remained unchanged. As states moved quickly after the Dobbs decision to enact abortion bans and strict gestational limits, public opinion moved in the opposite direction. Today, more Americans identify as pro-choice than they did before Dobbs. And, as we document in our book, more Americans are now taking absolutist positions. They support legal access to abortion in all or most cases and oppose government regulation altogether. One of the most striking changes in the post-Dobbs era concerns who cares most about abortion. For decades, abortion was a higher priority for Republicans and those identifying as pro-life. That dynamic has now flipped. In both 2022 and 2024, Democrats and pro-choice Americans were more likely than Republicans to say abortion was a top political issue shaping their vote. In our book, we document how in both 2022 and 2024, pro-choice Democrats were especially motivated to vote and remained highly loyal to Democratic candidates. At the same time, the considerable minority of Republicans who support legal abortion found themselves politically cross-pressured, meaning they experienced conflicting political influences. Drawing on multiple nationally representative data sets, our book reveals that roughly one-third of Republicans hold views on abortion that do not align with the official pro-life position embraced by their party. They either identify as pro-choice or support legal abortion in at least some cases. It was one thing to identify as a pro-choice Republican when Roe guaranteed a constitutional right to abortion. After Dobbs, however, Republican electoral victories could directly result in abortion bans and other restrictions. That makes partisan choices far more consequential. We found that cross-pressured Republicans had lower turnout rates and were more willing to cross party lines, reflecting the growing tension between their abortion views and their party’s position. Given the size of this group, that presents a serious challenge for GOP candidates. At the same time, efforts to find a middle ground on abortion have proven difficult. Republican legislators in North Carolina and Virginia, for example, have sought to position policies such as 12- or 15-week bans as a reasonable compromise. That might have worked in 1990. But public opinion has shifted in ways that make this strategy increasingly untenable. Our research shows that most Americans, including Republicans, do not see these “moderate” policies as meaningfully different from more restrictive bans. One reason may be that, in the wake of Dobbs, abortion restrictions have become concrete rather than abstract. Extensive media coverage of women denied care during miscarriages, severe pregnancy complications and other medical emergencies has highlighted the consequences of gestational limits. This leads many Americans to judge these policies by their practical effects rather than the specific week at which abortion is prohibited. In addition, our original survey data reveals that many Americans have only a limited understanding of how pregnancy is dated. That makes distinctions between six-, 12- and 15-week bans less meaningful than policymakers often assume. Another major change is the emergence of a gender gap in abortion attitudes. For decades, men and women held remarkably similar views on abortion. That is no longer the case. Since Dobbs, women have become significantly more supportive of abortion rights than men. For example, 56% of women say abortion should be legal in all or most circumstances, compared to 41% of men. This new gender gap reflects both women’s experiences with pregnancy and abortion and the changed policy environment following Dobbs. After the ruling, the consequences of abortion restrictions became far more immediate and tangible. Rather than accepting these new restrictions, many women reacted against them. As abortion policy moved sharply to the right in many states, women’s attitudes moved in the opposite direction. This has resulted in substantially greater support for abortion rights. Our survey research further finds that a better understanding of human reproduction, including how pregnancies are dated, is associated with greater support for legal access to abortion. Taken together, these changes have reshaped American politics in ways that advantage Democrats. Abortion rights played a key role in the 2022 midterms, contributing to stronger-than-expected Democratic performance nationwide. And it continues to shape voter motivation and turnout patterns heading into future elections. That said, abortion is not the only issue that matters in modern U.S. politics. In the 2026 midterm elections, the economy and partisanship – especially in an era dominated by President Donald Trump – will remain central to electoral outcomes. Abortion alone is unlikely to determine any single race. But it has altered the political landscape in ways that will matter this November and beyond. The phrase that gives our book its title – “Not Going Back” – captures this moment. The changes we document are not temporary reactions to a single Supreme Court decision. The stability that defined abortion politics for half a century is gone. The new normal is a political landscape in which abortion rights have become both more widely supported and more politically consequential. They are motivating Democratic voters while creating new tensions within the Republican coalition. Perhaps most importantly, Dobbs transformed abortion from a constitutional question into an electoral one. As abortion laws became substantially more restrictive, public opinion moved toward greater support for abortion access. The 2026 elections will offer another test of how the U.S. responds when public policy and public preferences move in opposite directions.
